feedback: If the learner expects the queen to assign jobs: 'The worker doesn't wait for orders — bees take on the jobs the colony needs by instinct. The queen's job is laying eggs.'
Encourage consequence reasoning: 'Good question to ask — if no bee did the foraging, the whole hive would run out of food.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each worker takes on several jobs that the colony needs, and does so without being commanded — building a fuller picture of how the colony self-organises.
learnerActions: Interview a worker bee (in role) about the different jobs it does through its life — cleaning, nursing the young, building comb, guarding, and foraging.
Ask what would happen to the hive if no bees did one of those jobs.
Ask whether the queen tells the worker what to do, and compare the answer to what you expected.
activities.title: A day in the hive: ask a worker about its jobs

feedback: Correct answer to the boss claim: 'It's not really right — the queen is not a boss giving orders. Her main job is to lay the eggs. The workers find food, build and clean tunnels, care for the eggs and young, and guard the nest. Living in a colony helps because the jobs are shared out, so no single ant has to do everything and the whole colony survives better than one ant could alone.'
If a child says every ant does the same job: 'Look again — different ants do different jobs: the queen lays eggs while workers forage, build, and guard. That sharing of jobs is the key idea.'
If a child says one ant could survive just as well alone: 'A single ant would have to do every job at once — find food, guard, and tend young. The colony survives better because the work is shared.'
On naming two different jobs: 'Good — a queen laying eggs and a worker foraging are two different jobs; having different members on different tasks is what lets the colony cover everything at once.'
On the bee-hive transfer: 'A hive is organised the same way — a queen laying eggs and workers sharing out the jobs. It's the same division-of-labour idea in a different social insect.'
activities.intendedInsight: Children who understand social insects give the queen the egg-laying role (not a command role), explain that dividing up the jobs lets the colony do more than any single ant could, and recognise that a bee hive is organised in the same division-of-labour way.
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic: 'In an ant nest there is a queen and lots of worker ants. Someone says: The queen is the boss — she tells all the other ants what to do. Is that right? Tell me what the queen actually does and what the workers do, and why living together in a colony helps the ants.'
Match each member to its role (queen to laying eggs; worker to foraging/building/guarding/nursing).
Answer a consequence question: 'What happens to the colony if there are no foragers at all?'
Answer the follow-up: 'Why does living together in a colony help, compared with one ant on its own?'
Name two DIFFERENT jobs in the colony and say why it helps that they are different.
Transfer the idea: 'A bee hive also has a queen and workers. Is a hive organised like the ant nest, or differently?'
activities.title: Check your thinking: roles and what fails without them
